tips.title: Check where the emergency exits are before you enter a bar, a club or an escape room; if they are locked or blocked, pick another venue
tips.cost: No cost at all. Ten seconds looking around as you walk in.
tips.inPlainWords: India has no single national law that spells out exit rules for every bar, club or escape room: fire safety is a state subject, and a venue is licensed and inspected under the state fire rules, the municipal by-laws and, for a large building, the National Building Code of India 2016. What that means in practice is simple: an exit that is locked, blocked by stacked chairs or crates, or hidden behind a curtain is a defect in the premises, and the person to tell is the local fire officer or the municipal licence department, not only the manager. If a private room is in a basement, has only one way out, or the corridor is cluttered, choose a different venue.
tips.benefit: A licensed venue is required to keep its means of escape usable and its exit signs lit, and the state fire service issues the no-objection certificate on which the trade licence depends. The National Building Code of India 2016 sets out the exit widths, travel distances and signage a building is designed to, and states adopt it through their fire rules. A licensed place that fails an inspection can lose the licence, which is why a complaint to the fire officer carries weight. Escape rooms and clubs in converted houses are the ones most often outside that system entirely.
tips.sources: National Building Code of India 2016, Bureau of Indian Standards. <https://www.bis.gov.in/>; Consumer Protection Act, 2019. <https://www.indiacode.nic.in/>
tips.caveats: If any of these is present, pick another venue: a private room underground, only one exit, a corridor filled with clutter, or an exit light that is dead. In a fire at such a place, smoke, narrow corridors and a crowd that has been drinking make escape far harder than it looks from the doorway — you may have seconds. Look for the exit before you sit down, and count the doors between your seat and the street.

tips.title: Ask for the price card before you order and keep the bill — an extra added at the end is the part you can actually dispute
tips.cost: No cost. Ask for the price list before ordering, and keep the bill.
tips.inPlainWords: There is no single central rule that makes every restaurant or venue in India display its prices. Packaged goods are the part the law covers clearly: the Legal Metrology (Packaged Commodities) Rules, 2011 require the retail sale price, the quantity and the manufacturer's details to be printed on the pack, and a shop may not charge above that price. For a restaurant or a venue, ask for the menu or the rate card before you order, and confirm the price of anything sold by weight or at 'market rate' before it is cooked. A service charge is not compulsory: the Department of Consumer Affairs' 2022 guidelines say it may not be levied automatically, and you can ask for it to be removed. A false or misleading price is an unfair trade practice under the Consumer Protection Act, 2019; keep the bill and complain to the National Consumer Helpline on 1915.
tips.benefit: The Consumer Protection Act, 2019 covers a false or misleading price and a deficient service, and a complaint can go to the district consumer commission for a refund and compensation. The bill should show the tax and the total. For a packaged item the printed retail sale price is the ceiling. For a restaurant, the practical protection is the price you were shown plus the bill: ask what the 'market price' dish costs before it is cooked, and ask for the service charge to be taken off if you do not want to pay it.
tips.sources: Consumer Protection Act, 2019. <https://www.indiacode.nic.in/>; Department of Consumer Affairs, guidelines on service charge. <https://consumeraffairs.nic.in/>; Legal Metrology (Packaged Commodities) Rules, 2011. <https://consumeraffairs.nic.in/>; National Consumer Helpline. <https://consumerhelpline.gov.in/>
tips.caveats: A 'market price' item should be quoted before cooking. A service charge is not a tip and is not compulsory: the 2022 guidelines say it must not be levied automatically, so ask for it to be removed. A venue's 'minimum charge' should be shown before you sit down.

tips.title: If someone offers you drugs at a venue, leave — possession is an offence in India, and a room you booked is your responsibility
tips.cost: No cost at all. Just stand up and walk away. The hard part is having to leave in front of a whole group of people.
tips.inPlainWords: Under the Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances Act, 1985, it is an offence to produce, possess, sell, buy, transport or use a narcotic drug or a psychotropic substance, and the punishment depends on the quantity seized — small, commercial or intermediate — and on the substance. There is no separate 'public order' penalty here: even a first offence with a small quantity can mean prison, and a commercial quantity carries a much heavier sentence decided by a special court. A venue that allows drug use on its premises risks its excise and police licence. If someone offers you an unknown powder, a pill or a vape cartridge, walk away right then.
tips.benefit: The Act classifies quantities and the sentence follows the class; consumption is dealt with separately, and abetment and conspiracy are offences in their own right, so 'I only passed it on' is not a defence. The seizing officer can arrest and the case is tried by a special court. A bar or club that breaches its licence conditions can lose its excise licence, and that is the leverage a complaint to the excise or police licensing authority uses. None of this makes the venue the judge: your own possession is the offence you carry.
tips.sources: Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances Act, 1985. <https://www.indiacode.nic.in/>; Central Bureau of Narcotics. <https://cbn.nic.in/>
tips.caveats: If anyone offers you unknown powders, pills or vape cartridges to try, leave immediately — do not stay to watch. Individual liability is heavier than the venue's: possession is the offence, and a room you booked or a flat you share is where the search happens. 'It was not mine' is a defence that has to be proved. If a friend collapses after taking something, call 112 and stay with them; the medical emergency comes before the legal question.

tips.title: Do not accept candy or snacks from strangers, do not drink a beverage you left unattended, and do not take a vape cartridge handed to you by someone else
tips.cost: No cost at all. Never accept anything offered by others. If your own cup has been out of sight, simply get a new one.
tips.inPlainWords: The drugs that turn up in drinks and vapes are not the ones people picture. The reported cases involve sedatives and vape liquid spiked with a synthetic cannabinoid, and the point of spiking is robbery or assault, not a joke. Giving someone a drug without their knowledge is an offence under the Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances Act, 1985, and so is possessing it; the sentence depends on the substance and the quantity and is decided by a court. There is no published fine table for drugging someone. Any drink that has been out of your sight should be replaced, not finished.
tips.benefit: Synthetic cannabinoids are controlled as psychotropic substances under the NDPS Act, and its schedules are amended by notification as new compounds appear, so a cartridge that was not covered last year may be now. A spiked drink is usually about robbery or sexual assault: the drug makes the victim compliant and the memory unreliable, and what is lost is the phone, the cash and the account passwords. Replacing a drink is cheap; a blood or urine test after the fact is not, and it has to be done within hours to be useful.
tips.sources: Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances Act, 1985. <https://www.indiacode.nic.in/>; Central Bureau of Narcotics. <https://cbn.nic.in/>
tips.caveats: This applies at a school gate, a friend's party and on a long-distance bus, not only at a bar, and it works the same whether the offer is candy, a drink or a vape cartridge. After being drugged, victims often lose money, a phone, or worse; no Indian statistic reliably counts it, so treat it as a warning drawn from cases rather than a rate. If you feel suddenly and inexplicably drunk, tell someone you trust and get to a hospital — a test in the first hours is the evidence. For unknown powders or cartridges found in such a setting, see item 3.

tips.title: Avoid escape rooms and scripted mystery games in residential buildings or below the first basement
tips.cost: No cost involved. Just ask for the building floor number before booking.
tips.inPlainWords: India has no rule aimed specifically at escape rooms or scripted mystery games. What applies is the ordinary licensing chain: a commercial entertainment premises needs a trade licence from the municipal body, a fire no-objection certificate from the state fire service, and a police licence under the state police or places-of-public-resort rules. A game run out of a flat is outside all of it. The risk is structural: a basement room with one stair, partitions that make a maze, props that burn, and doors that are meant to be opened by solving a puzzle. Before you book, ask what floor it is on and whether the building is commercial.
tips.benefit: A fire no-objection certificate is issued against a specific premises and a specific use, and a residential flat cannot hold one for a public entertainment use; the state fire rules and the National Building Code of India 2016 set the travel distance, exit width and signage that a basement needs. A venue that cannot show a trade licence and a fire certificate is running on the assumption that nothing will go wrong. The same logic applies to a club or a banquet hall in a converted house.
tips.sources: National Building Code of India 2016, Bureau of Indian Standards. <https://www.bis.gov.in/>; Consumer Protection Act, 2019. <https://www.indiacode.nic.in/>
tips.caveats: These places are usually dark, cut into small rooms, full of flammable props, and the door sometimes needs a puzzle solved to open. In a fire that is far harder to escape than from an ordinary shop. You can check the floor and the building type on a review page before booking, but the licence is the real test: ask to see it, and walk away if the answer is a shrug. If the only exit you can find is the one you came in by, leave.

tips.title: Going for a brisk walk or a jog when feeling down: the effect size of exercise on depression is proportional to its intensity
tips.cost: Free. Each session takes about half an hour. The hard part is that when you’re in a bad mood, moving feels the last thing you want to do — you have to push yourself to get started.
tips.inPlainWords: This study pooled data from 218 randomized trials involving over 14,000 adults with major depressive disorder. The biggest improvements were seen with brisk walking or jogging. Yoga, strength training, mixed aerobic workouts, and tai chi/Qigong also showed benefits, with fairly similar effect sizes across these activities. Generally, the higher the exercise intensity, the better the outcome; however, strength training and yoga tend to be the easiest to stick with long-term. The authors themselves note that the overall evidence quality is relatively low, but the key takeaway is that any physical activity is better than none — pick whatever type you’re most likely to keep doing.
tips.benefit: This result comes from combining data across 218 randomized controlled trials split into two groups, covering 495 treatment arms and 14,170 participants who met clinical criteria for major depression. A Bayesian network meta-analysis was used to compare all these different forms of exercise against each other, using standard care or placebo pills as control groups. The effect size is expressed as Hedges’ g; the more negative this value, the greater the symptom improvement. For brisk walking or jogging, the value was −0.62 (95% confidence interval: −0.80 to −0.45). Yoga came in at −0.55 (−0.73 to −0.36), strength training at −0.49 (−0.69 to −0.29), mixed aerobic exercise at −0.43 (−0.61 to −0.24), and tai chi/Qigong at −0.42 (−0.65 to −0.21). The original paper states that “the effect of exercise is directly proportional to its intensity”, meaning higher intensity yields better results. Strength training and yoga also score highest on acceptability, making them the most sustainable choices for most people.
tips.sources: Noetel M, Sanders T, Gallardo-Gómez D, et al. (2024). Effect of exercise for depression: systematic review and network meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials. BMJ, 384, e075847. <https://doi.org/10.1136/bmj-2023-075847>
tips.caveats: This finding is somewhat controversial. The authors themselves point out that only one out of the 218 studies met sufficiently rigorous design standards to rule out major bias. Using standard grading criteria, brisk walking and jogging only qualify for a “low” confidence rating, while all other exercise types receive “very low” ratings. Since participants know they’re taking part in an exercise program, placebo effects inevitably play a role, skewing results upward. Still, the overall conclusion holds up: any physical activity is better than none, intensity should be kept reasonably high, and you should choose a type you can realistically stick with over time. This section expands on the earlier advice in Section 3 to “get moving when feeling down”, but it is by no means a substitute for professional medical treatment after a proper diagnosis.

tips.title: When anxiety interferes with daily life, mindfulness‑based stress reduction works just as well as common anti‑anxiety drugs
tips.cost: Taking a course costs a bit of money. The program lasts eight weeks, with one class per week plus daily home practice. The real challenge is keeping up with that daily practice for the whole eight weeks.
tips.inPlainWords: 276 adults diagnosed with anxiety disorder were randomly split into two groups. One group attended an eight‑week mindfulness‑based stress reduction course, while the other took escitalopram. At the end, symptom improvement was almost identical in both groups. The difference showed up in side effects: almost 80 % of the medication group experienced at least one adverse reaction, and ten people dropped out because of this. In the course group, about 15 % reported side effects, but no one left the program. The program used a standardized eight‑week curriculum — it isn’t the same as any random meditation app you might download.
tips.benefit: This was a non‑inferiority randomized controlled trial conducted at three academic medical centers in the United States, designed to see whether the course performed as well as medication. 276 participants were assigned 1:1 to either an eight‑week mindfulness‑based stress reduction program or escitalopram at a flexible dose of 10–20 mg. 208 people completed the whole study. Using a clinician‑rated scale of anxiety severity, the mindfulness group showed a reduction of 1.35 points versus 1.43 points for the drug group. The difference between the two groups was −0.07 (95 % CI −0.38 to 0.23; P = 0.65), meaning the gap is statistically indistinguishable from zero. This value stayed above the pre‑set non‑inferiority threshold of −0.495. Side‑effect rates differed markedly: 78.6 % of the medication group experienced at least one trial‑related adverse event, leading to ten withdrawals, while only 15.4 % of the course group reported any side effects and no one dropped out.
tips.sources: Hoge EA, Bui E, Mete M, Dutton MA, Baker AW, Simon NM (2023). Mindfulness-based stress reduction vs escitalopram for the treatment of adults with anxiety disorders: a randomized clinical trial. JAMA Psychiatry, 80(1), 13-21. <https://doi.org/10.1001/jamapsychiatry.2022.3679>
tips.caveats: The trial employed a standardized eight‑week mindfulness‑based stress reduction curriculum (MBSR), not a generic meditation app; the two cannot be equated. This recommendation applies to individuals who already meet diagnostic criteria for anxiety disorder; they should still consult a physician. Its practical value lies in offering a treatment option with comparable evidence strength for those who hesitate to take medication because of potential side effects.

tips.title: For quick relief on the spot, try the 5‑minute “cyclic sigh”: two inhalations followed by a prolonged exhalation
tips.cost: No cost at all. Just 5 minutes a day.
tips.inPlainWords: In a one‑month controlled trial where participants performed each of three breathing exercises for 5 minutes daily, all three proved more effective than an equal amount of mindfulness meditation at lifting mood and lowering respiratory rate. The “cyclic sigh” — which emphasizes lengthening the exhale — performed best. The method is simple: inhale once through the nose, then take a brief second inhale to fully fill the lungs, and finally exhale slowly through the mouth. This particular study relied on self‑reported data and involved a relatively small group of volunteers, yet it required zero expense.
tips.benefit: This home‑based, randomized controlled trial compared three distinct 5‑minute daily breathing routines — cyclic sighing (focused on extended exhalation), box breathing (equal durations of inhale, hold, and exhale), and cyclic hyperventilation with pauses — against an equivalent mindfulness meditation regimen over a month. Using a mixed‑effects model on pooled data, each breathing technique outperformed meditation; cyclic sighing stood out for its superior impact on mood improvement (statistically significant at P<0.05) and on reducing breathing frequency (also P<0.05).
tips.sources: Balban MY, Neri E, Kogon MM, et al. (2023). Brief structured respiration practices enhance mood and reduce physiological arousal. Cell Reports Medicine, 4(1), 100895. <https://doi.org/10.1016/j.xcrm.2022.100895>
tips.caveats: Execute the exercise by inhaling once through the nose, briefly adding a second inhale to maximize lung expansion, then exhale gently and fully through the mouth for a full 5 minutes. Although this trial was conducted at home, relied on participant self‑assessment, and involved a modest sample size, its benefits are clear: it costs nothing, takes only five minutes, can be done anywhere, and offers modest but tangible advantages over standard mindfulness practice.

tips.title: Treat “regular social contact” as a health expense — don’t wait until you’re feeling down to reach out
tips.cost: It requires some money and time to arrange meetups. The hard part is making the effort to schedule them even when you’re in a good mood.
tips.inPlainWords: Long-term epidemiological research tracking over 3 million people for an average of 7 years demonstrates the vital role of social connection. Those experiencing social isolation had a roughly 30% higher risk of dying during that period compared to non-isolated individuals. People reporting loneliness faced a 25% higher risk, while those living alone faced a 30% higher risk. These figures are similar in magnitude and are even more pronounced among people under 65. Keep in mind these are observational data; it’s also possible that people in poorer health are more likely to end up isolated.
tips.benefit: As noted, this is a meta-analysis of 70 studies with 3.4 million participants observed over 7 years. Social isolation, loneliness, and living alone all correlate with higher mortality. After adjusting for age and health status, the weighted average risk ratios were: 1.29 for social isolation, 1.26 for loneliness, and 1.32 for living alone. In other words, each condition raised the risk of dying during the study period by roughly 30%, 25%, and 30% respectively. The effects are comparable across all three factors and are stronger in younger adults.
tips.sources: Holt-Lunstad J, Smith TB, Baker M, Harris T, Stephenson D (2015). Loneliness and social isolation as risk factors for mortality: a meta-analytic review. Perspectives on Psychological Science, 10(2), 227-237. <https://doi.org/10.1177/1745691614568352>
tips.caveats: This topic remains debated. These findings are purely correlational; no randomized controlled trials have been conducted to prove cause and effect. It’s also true that people with poorer health are more likely to become isolated or have fewer social interactions. The authors argue that social relationships are as important to health as smoking or obesity, yet there’s no randomized evidence showing that increasing social contact actually lowers mortality. This point does not contradict Section 3’s advice to “cut back on draining relationships”; that section focuses on eliminating toxic connections, while this one stresses the value of maintaining those that replenish your energy.

tips.title: Living near green spaces means you can use them for walking, strolling, or just sitting around
tips.cost: No cost at all — it’s free and easy to incorporate into daily life.
tips.inPlainWords: Nine studies from seven countries involving 8.32 million people show that for every 0.1 increase in the normalized vegetation index (NDVI) within 500 meters of a home, the risk of dying during the same period drops by roughly 4%. This measures greenery right around where people live, not how often they visit parks. Naturally, neighborhoods with more greenery tend to have wealthier residents and cleaner air. So don’t interpret this as “visiting parks automatically adds years to your life”; the practical takeaway is to consider nearby green spaces when choosing where to live.
tips.benefit: This result comes from a meta-analysis of nine long-term cohort studies spanning seven countries and 8.32 million participants. It looks at vegetation levels within 500 meters of residences, quantified via NDVI — a number that reflects ground-level greenery (bare soil or concrete scores near 0, dense vegetation near 1). A 0.1 rise in NDVI corresponds to a pooled hazard ratio of 0.96 for overall mortality (95% CI 0.94–0.97), meaning a roughly 4% reduction in death risk — with actual values likely falling between 3% and 6%. Seven out of the nine studies found lower mortality in greener areas, a pattern unlikely to be coincidental; the other two showed no clear link.
tips.sources: Rojas-Rueda D, Nieuwenhuijsen MJ, Gascon M, Perez-Leon D, Mudu P (2019). Green spaces and mortality: a systematic review and meta-analysis of cohort studies. The Lancet Planetary Health, 3(11), e469-e477. <https://doi.org/10.1016/S2542-5196(19)30215-3>
tips.caveats: This finding remains debated. The studies themselves vary widely in results (I² = 95%, indicating substantial disagreement), and the analysis tracks neighborhood greenery rather than personal park visits. Moreover, greener areas typically feature higher incomes, cleaner air, and more active lifestyles — all factors intertwined with vegetation levels. Again, don’t read this as “parks guarantee longer life”; the key insight is that living near green spaces costs nothing and may offer health benefits. NDVI is simply a numeric way to gauge local greenery, where values near 0 represent barren or paved zones and values near 1 indicate lush vegetation — so a 0.1 increase roughly equals moving from a bare urban block to one lined with trees.

tips.title: Do not use hot springs, saunas, or hot baths after drinking alcohol
tips.cost: Free. Saves money by postponing spa or hot bath visits to a sober day; take a quick lukewarm shower instead. The friction is social pressure, as hot springs or saunas often follow group drinking dinners.
tips.inPlainWords: In Finland, half of all sauna-related deaths involve alcohol consumption. In Tokyo, post-mortem forensic records show about one-quarter of bath-related fatalities had significant blood alcohol levels, with intoxication being the single most common trigger for bathtub drowning. Public health agencies strictly advise against hot baths, saunas, or thermal spas after drinking. Never let an intoxicated companion bathe or enter a sauna alone.
tips.benefit: Forensic analyses in Finland examining all sauna-related deaths from 1990 to 2002 using police and medical examiner records found that approximately 50% of decedents were under the influence of alcohol at the time of death, highlighting alcohol as the primary modifiable fatal risk factor. In Tokyo, Japan, medical examiners reviewed 3,289 sudden bath-related deaths occurring between 2009 and 2011; among 550 autopsied cases, 140 (approx. 25.5%) had blood alcohol concentrations exceeding 0.5 mg/mL. In a forensic series of 77 bathtub drowning fatalities in Tokyo, acute alcohol intoxication was identified as the leading contributing factor (25 cases), surpassing pre-existing heart disease (22 cases). The Consumer Affairs Agency of Japan reported 7,776 domestic bathtub drowning deaths in 2024 (7,363 among adults over 65), issuing explicit safety guidelines cautioning that bathing immediately after meals, alcohol intake, or sedating medication drastically elevates fatal risk. The mechanism is the same everywhere: hot water and a hot room dilate the peripheral blood vessels, blood pressure falls, and the brain is briefly under-perfused, which is why an intoxicated person can black out in a bath or on a sauna bench.
tips.sources: Kenttämies A, Karkola K (2008). Death in sauna. Journal of Forensic Sciences, 53(3), 724-729. <https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1556-4029.2008.00703.x>; Suzuki H, Hikiji W, Tanifuji T, Abe N, Fukunaga T (2015). Characteristics of sudden bath-related death investigated by medical examiners in Tokyo, Japan. Journal of Epidemiology, 25(2), 126-132. <https://doi.org/10.2188/jea.JE20140068>; Mishima S, Suzuki H, Fukunaga T, Nishitani Y (2018). Postmortem computed tomography findings in cases of bath-related death: applicability and limitation in forensic practice. Forensic Science International, 282, 195-203. <https://doi.org/10.1016/j.forsciint.2017.11.030>; Consumer Affairs Agency of Japan (2025). Caution regarding elderly accidents during New Year holidays: Avoid bathing immediately after meals, drinking, or medication. <https://www.caa.go.jp/policies/policy/consumer_safety/caution/caution_084/>
tips.caveats: Graded B because the evidence is derived from post-mortem forensic series and epidemiological registries of fatalities rather than randomized trials. While absolute bathtub and sauna deaths are relatively infrequent, alcohol involvement accounts for 25% to 50% of observed fatalities across jurisdictions. While bathtub drownings predominantly affect older adults, sauna-related cardiovascular syncope and hyperthermia frequently affect younger intoxicated adults. For evidence-based benefits, temperature, and duration of routine bathing, see Chapter 2, Rule 36. For caring for an intoxicated individual, see Chapter 13, Rule 46.

tips.title: Wear certified sports helmets when skiing, snowboarding, rollerblading, or cycling
tips.cost: A certified bicycle helmet costs upwards of a thousand rupees, and a ski or snowboard helmet more; the cost of using it is five seconds to buckle it before each session.
tips.inPlainWords: Wearing a helmet while skiing or snowboarding reduces the risk of head injury by roughly one-third (and by nearly 60% in children under 13). When cycling, wearing a helmet cuts severe traumatic brain injury by nearly 70% and fatal head injury by 65%. Helmets do not increase the risk of neck injuries.
tips.benefit: A meta-analysis of 12 studies on skiing and snowboarding injuries found that helmet use was associated with a 35% reduction in head injuries (odds ratio OR 0.65; 95% CI 0.55–0.79). Among children under 13, the protective effect was even greater, reducing head injuries by 59% (OR 0.41; 95% CI 0.27–0.59). Helmet use did not increase neck injury risk (OR 0.89; 95% CI 0.72–1.09). For cycling, a systematic review and meta-analysis of 40 studies covering over 64,000 injured cyclists found that helmet use reduced head injury by 51% (OR 0.49; 95% CI 0.42–0.57), severe head injury by 69% (OR 0.31; 95% CI 0.25–0.37), and fatal head injury by 65% (OR 0.35; 95% CI 0.14–0.88). Facial injuries were reduced by 33% (OR 0.67; 95% CI 0.56–0.81), with no significant association with neck trauma (OR 0.96; 95% CI 0.74–1.25). No Indian law requires a helmet on a ski slope — India has very few organised ski areas and no national ski helmet rule — but the rental shop and the ski school usually require one, and the helmet protects you whatever the rule says.
tips.sources: Russell K, Christie J, Hagel BE (2010). The effect of helmets on the risk of head and neck injuries among skiers and snowboarders: a meta-analysis. CMAJ, 182(4), 333-340. <https://doi.org/10.1503/cmaj.091080>; Olivier J, Creighton P (2017). Bicycle injuries and helmet use: a systematic review and meta-analysis. International Journal of Epidemiology, 46(1), 278-292. <https://doi.org/10.1093/ije/dyw153>; Department of Consumer Affairs. <https://consumeraffairs.nic.in/>
tips.caveats: Helmets reduce head trauma upon impact; they do not prevent falls or collisions themselves. Rollerblading and skateboarding share similar impact physics, supporting helmet adoption. Ensure helmets fit snugly and the chinstrap is securely fastened; when renting gear, try on multiple sizes for proper fit. For motorcycle and electric bicycle helmet guidelines, see Chapter 1, Rule 2.
